title: How Much Track Is Left For SNOW Stock?
detail:
How Much Track Is Left For SNOW Stock?
Trefis Team
Thu, August 27, 2026 at 4:14 PM PDT 4 min read

ORCL-PD
AMZN
GOOG
PLTR
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image by Gerd Altmann from Pixabay

A powerful business engine has fueled this data stock's long-term run, but a recent pullback forces every investor to ask if the ticket price already accounts for the journey ahead.

Snowflake (SNOW) has been a genuine runner, the kind of stock that makes you feel you are missing out. Its long-term trend strength ranks in the top 7% of large U.S. stocks. But the fear of chasing a hot name is met with an immediate reality check: the stock is not at its peak. It trades about 7% below its 52-week high and has pulled back about 7% from its one-month high, so the weakness is fresh. The stock also sits about 7% below its two-year high of $337.38. This presents the classic momentum question for any would-be buyer: is this a brief pause in a powerful climb, or has the market already priced in all the good news? Momentum with fuel, or momentum fully priced?

This run is powered by a real business engine.

The source of Snowflake's momentum extends beyond its stock chart. The company's AI Data Cloud platform is seeing surging demand as enterprises race to deploy artificial intelligence. Revenue over the last twelve months grew 31%, a stark contrast to the S&P 500 median of 8.4%. The company is also generating cash, with an operating cash flow margin of 25%, beating the market median of 22%.

The fuel for this is the rapid adoption of new AI-centric products. Management noted on its latest earnings call that tools like Snowflake Intelligence and Cortex Code (CoCo) are seeing "the fastest adoption of any new products in our history." This does more than add a new revenue line; it's creating a flywheel. Customers using these tools are increasing their use of the core data platform, which prompted management to raise its full-year product revenue growth outlook for fiscal 2027 to 31%.

The market charges a steep price for that power.

A buyer today is paying a premium for that growth. Snowflake trades at a price-to-sales multiple of 21.6, far above the S&P 500 median of 3.3. Profitability remains a work in progress; the company's operating margin over the last twelve months is -26%, compared to the S&P 500 median of 18.5%. The market is clearly betting that Snowflake's current investments will translate into future profits.

Beyond being a valuation concern, the honest catch here is a business risk. As one recent analysis notes, there is a question of whether this growth arrives at a lower gross margin. Management confirms its new AI products have a lower gross margin than its core platform. The bigger risk is customer behavior. Investors worry that as clients see their bills rise from the consumption-based pricing of these powerful AI tools, they might "govern or throttle the use" to contain spending. If the cost of innovation outpaces the perceived value, the growth engine could sputter.

Photo by athree23 on Pixabay

The customers, the contracts, and the expansion rate behind Palantir's run were all on the record before the price moved, and the options market had stopped bracing for a big move.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock returned 34% over the three months through late August, against 2.1% for the S&P 500. The August 3 second-quarter report got the credit. But nearly everything it confirmed had already been signed, filed or said out loud by early May. The run was legible in advance.

Stellantis, The USDA And Cleveland-Cliffs All Signed First

In late March the company renewed and expanded its Stellantis partnership for another five years, broadening Stellantis's use of Palantir Foundry and adding Palantir's AI platform. In April the USDA awarded a contract of up to $300 million to secure farmland and modernize its services to farmers, and Cleveland-Cliffs signed a three-year deal putting Palantir's AI at the center of its own operations and commercial processes. Trailing-twelve-month revenue as of fiscal Q1 2026 was $5.22 billion, so none of this was transformative alone; what mattered was that all three were agreed before the price moved.

The Expansion Rate Climbed Across Three Quarters

Contracts are lumpy. The cleaner tell was net dollar retention, which tracks what existing customers spend against a year earlier, excluding anyone won in the past twelve months. Retention ran 134% for fiscal Q3 2025 and 139% for fiscal Q4 2025, then jumped 1,100 basis points to 150% for fiscal Q1 2026, the largest step in that run and on the record in early May. That climb is not a forecast about AI; it is customers who already bought paying for more. The growth was profitable too: trailing operating margin as of fiscal Q1 2026 was 38.1%, against a three-year average of 14.2%. Growth arriving with margins like that is the combination the Trefis High Quality Portfolio looks for in its holdings.

AI Sovereignty Was A New Label On Old Momentum

The thesis predates August too. In early May the company's revenue chief framed the opportunity as enterprises waking up to the risk of being beholden to models alone. On August 3 that got a name and a number: U.S. commercial revenue up 149% year over year to $764 million in fiscal Q2 2026, and full-year 2026 revenue guidance raised to a midpoint of $8.154 billion, representing 82% growth year over year and an 11-point increase over the prior guide's growth rate. Management calls the demand "AI sovereignty," meaning customers who want their data, logic, and security under their own control, not an outside lab's. Demand kept arriving after fiscal Q2 2026 closed: the Sovereignty Bootcamps have drawn nearly 200 organizations, with a second announced on August 19.

title: Peter Thiel Has Steadily Sold Down His Palantir Stake for Years, Yet Remains Its Largest Individual Shareholder. Here's What His Selling Pattern Signals for Investors.
detail:
Peter Thiel Has Steadily Sold Down His Palantir Stake for Years, Yet Remains Its Largest Individual Shareholder. Here's What His Selling Pattern Signals for Investors.
Chris Neiger, The Motley Fool
Thu, August 27, 2026 at 6:00 AM PDT 4 min read
PLTR
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

It's often a wise strategy to watch the stock buying and selling patterns of company insiders. Sometimes, a ramp-up in selling by executives means that leadership is losing faith in their company. By contrast, a rush of share purchases can indicate that insiders are bullish on the company's future.

But interpreting those stock buys and stock sales isn't always straightforward.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Billionaire investor Peter Thiel was a co-founder of Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR), and he has sold millions of shares of the data analytics giant worth billions of dollars in total over the past few years.

Some investors have seen this as a warning sign. But they're probably reading too much into those sales. Here's why.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Thiel has sold millions of Palantir shares but still holds a 3% stake

Observant investors likely noticed that Thiel began selling large portions of his Palantir stake in early 2024. During that time, he unloaded tens of millions of shares.

His selling has continued since then. Most recently, in March of this year, he sold another 2 million shares, totaling about $290 million.

Thiel owned about 8% of Palantir back in 2020, but after all the selling, he has reduced his stake to about 3%.

Why Palantir investors shouldn't worry

All of this may seem troubling at first glance, but we should put his selling -- and his current stake -- into perspective.

First, Thiel has owned Palantir shares for more than two decades. That's a heck of a long time to hold a stock, and it's certainly a good indicator that he is a believer in Palantir and its highly profitable business.

Second, Thiel's stake in Palantir remains very large. While he's reduced his position, he still has a 3% stake in the company. Based on Palantir's current market cap of about $423 billion, that stake is worth about $12.7 billion.

Forbes lists Thiel's net worth at about $33 billion, which means more than one-third of his net worth is held in Palantir stock -- even after selling tens of millions of shares. In short, his fortunes are still very much entwined with Palantir's success.

All of which suggests that while he has sold a significant amount of Palantir stock over the past couple of years, he hasn't lost faith in the company. Thiel is still the chairman of Palantir's board, and his approximately 69 million shares give him the largest stake in the company among individual investors, far surpassing even CEO Alex Karp's holdings of about 6.4 million shares. It's worth mentioning, though, that despite his stake's small size relative to the total market cap of the company, because much of Karp's stake is held in special share classes, he (and Thiel, and Palantir President Stephen Cohen) retain substantial voting power within the company.
